# Conti Ransomware-as-a-Service: Organization, Leaks, and Public Attribution Record

## Executive summary

The returned public sources describe Conti as a large, commercially organized ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, also known as Wizard Spider, that used affiliates or other participants to conduct intrusions while maintaining centralized capabilities for malware development, testing, negotiation, administration, and data-leak operations. The sources characterize its extortion model as “double extortion”: stealing and encrypting data, then threatening to publish or sell the stolen material if the victim did not pay.

The February–March 2022 Conti chat disclosures provided unusually detailed visibility into the group’s internal business processes. The leaks reportedly included hundreds of JSON chat files, screenshots of tools, discussions of exploits and software design, credentials, and alleged infrastructure information. Public analysis of those materials described specialized business units, internal budgets, recruitment, testing, reverse engineering, penetration testing, ransom negotiation, and the use of outside contractors.

The attribution record is uneven. The U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice program officially described Conti/Wizard Spider as a Russian government-linked RaaS group and identified five online aliases—“Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” and “Dandis”—as actors believed to be linked to Conti. However, the returned sources do not establish the civilian identities behind those aliases or connect them to the individuals named in the Department of Justice records.

The Department of Justice records identify five defendants in two Conti-related federal cases: Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and Oleksii Lytvynenko. The four defendants charged in 2023 are described as charged, not convicted, and remain presumed innocent according to the DOJ page. Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on June 10, 2026, to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The available DOJ record does not map any of these defendants to the five Rewards for Justice aliases.

Accordingly, the public record supports a strong description of Conti’s operational model and internal commercialization, but it does not support a complete, verified identity map of the organization. Several important questions remain unresolved, including the identity of the leaker, the alias-to-defendant mappings, the precise nature of Conti’s relationship with the Russian government, and whether later smaller groups were organizational successors of Conti or merely related former personnel.

## 1. Scope and evidentiary status

This report is limited to the four source records returned by the benchmark tools:

- the U.S. Department of State’s Rewards for Justice profile;
- Rapid7’s analysis of the 2022 Conti chat disclosures;
- the Center for Internet Security’s analysis of the Conti leaks; and
- the U.S. Department of Justice’s Conti Ransomware case page.

The sources contain different types of evidence:

### 1.1 Government descriptions and procedural records

The Rewards for Justice page is an official U.S. government attribution and reward notice. It describes Conti as Russian government-linked and identifies aliases as actors “believed to be linked” to the group. That wording reflects an official attribution or intelligence assessment, not a judicial determination of the civilian identities behind those aliases. [Conti – Rewards for Justice](https://rewardsforjustice.net/rewards/conti/) [SRC-001]

The DOJ page is an official record of criminal charges and one guilty plea. Charges are allegations unless established in court. The page expressly states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. [Conti Ransomware](https://www.justice.gov/usao-mdtn/conti-ransomware-2) [SRC-004]

### 1.2 Threat-intelligence and investigative reporting

Rapid7’s account describes the contents and limitations of the leaked material and includes Rapid7 assessments about the possible identity or status of the leaker and Conti’s operational recovery. [Conti Ransomware Group Internal Chats Leaked Over Russia-Ukraine Conflict](https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2022/03/01/conti-ransomware-group-internal-chats-leaked-over-russia-ukraine-conflict/) [SRC-002]

The CIS account synthesizes leak analysis and cited KrebsOnSecurity reporting concerning Conti’s staffing, departments, budgets, procurement, and later fragmentation. These are investigative findings based on leaked material and reporting, not judicially adjudicated facts. [The Conti Leaks: A Case of Cybercrime’s Commercialization](https://www.cisecurity.org/insights/blog/the-conti-leaks-a-case-of-cybercrimes-commercialization) [SRC-003]

## 2. How the sources describe Conti as a RaaS operation

### 2.1 Centralized ransomware capability combined with distributed intrusion activity

The U.S. government describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as “a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) group” targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. [SRC-001]

The RaaS description implies a division of labor: a core operation maintains malware and related services, while affiliates or other participants conduct intrusions and share proceeds. CIS describes the general RaaS model as one in which groups lease malware to affiliates who carry out intrusions and share profits with developers. CIS refers to a commonly reported 70–30 division, but the returned source does not establish that every Conti arrangement used that exact percentage. [SRC-003]

This distinction is important. The evidence supports describing Conti as a service-based criminal enterprise, but it does not establish the terms of every affiliate relationship or show that all intrusions were conducted by independent affiliates.

### 2.2 Double extortion

CIS characterizes Conti’s model as double extortion. The two pressure mechanisms were:

1. encrypting the victim’s systems or data; and
2. threatening to publish or otherwise expose stolen data.

The Rewards for Justice page describes a similar workflow. Conti operators typically stole files, encrypted servers and workstations, demanded payment, directed victims to an online portal, and threatened to sell or publish the stolen information if payment was not made. Some ransom demands reportedly reached $25 million. [SRC-001] [SRC-003]

The leak-and-negotiation infrastructure was therefore not incidental to the malware. It was part of the commercial process by which the operation converted unauthorized access into revenue.

### 2.3 Scale and victim targeting

Rewards for Justice states that Conti was first detected in 2019 and had been used in more than 1,000 ransomware operations against U.S. and international critical infrastructure. It identifies law-enforcement agencies, emergency medical services, 9-1-1 dispatch centers, and municipalities among the targeted entities. The page also states that more than 400 organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States, were victimized in the healthcare and first-responder context. [SRC-001]

The DOJ page gives a different total, stating that Conti affected more than 900 businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims in the United States and around the world. [SRC-004]

These numbers should not be automatically combined. The sources may be using different time periods, victim categories, or counting methods. The returned materials do not resolve the discrepancy.

### 2.4 Commercial and corporate-style characteristics

The returned sources portray Conti as more than a loose collection of hackers. CIS reports that the leaks revealed features associated with a commercial organization:

- specialized departments;
- recruitment and human-resources functions;
- finance and accounting;
- internal budgets;
- product development;
- testing and quality control;
- customer-facing ransom negotiation; and
- procurement of commercial or dual-use tools.

CIS describes these features as evidence of the commercialization of cybercrime. [SRC-003]

Rapid7 similarly identifies a section of the leaked material describing Conti as a business and a well-funded one. The available source excerpt states that much of the chat traffic concerned ordinary business matters, although it does not provide a complete account of that section. [SRC-002]

## 3. What the Conti leaks reveal about internal organization

### 3.1 Provenance and limitations of the leaked material

Rapid7 reports that, on February 27, 2022, the Twitter account “@ContiLeaks” released a large collection of Conti chat logs. The first archive, `1.tgz`, reportedly contained:

- approximately 14 megabytes of chat logs;
- 393 JSON files;
- internal communications;
- screenshots of tools; and
- discussions of exploits and design processes.

Additional files were posted on February 28 and March 1, together with pro-Ukraine messages. [SRC-002]

The leaks were not complete. Rapid7 states that some messages were encrypted and unreadable. The evidence therefore provides a substantial but partial view of Conti’s internal operations.

The disclosed material also included usernames and passwords, alleged access information for command-and-control and stolen-data storage servers, and a file purporting to be Conti ransomware source code. Rapid7 did not access systems using the disclosed credentials and warned against doing so. The returned sources do not independently verify every credential, server detail, or purported source-code file. [SRC-002]

### 3.2 Specialized departments and roles

CIS reports that Conti divided its work into business units and recruited personnel for specific functions. The reported roles included:

- **Coders**, responsible for writing malicious code and integrating technologies;
- **Testers**, responsible for checking how payloads performed against security products;
- **Administrators**;
- **Reverse Engineers**;
- **Penetration Testers/Hackers**; and
- **Negotiators**, who coordinated ransom-payment discussions.

CIS also reports that spamming functions were contracted outside the organization. [SRC-003]

This evidence supports a functional model in which Conti separated malware development, operational intrusion, defensive testing, administration, and victim communications. It does not establish a complete hierarchy or demonstrate that each role corresponded to a single stable individual.

### 3.3 Staffing and internal resources

CIS reports that each department had its own budget, although units could borrow money from one another. A Conti insider cited in the account reportedly stated that the organization employed more than 60 people—mostly Coders and Testers—in July 2021. CIS also reports that staffing levels changed, including after internal security breaches. [SRC-003]

The staffing figure should be treated as an insider account rather than a verified census. It nevertheless reinforces the broader conclusion that Conti operated with a substantial workforce and differentiated labor.

### 3.4 Product development and technical quality control

The leaks reportedly showed a continuing effort to improve Conti’s ransomware product. CIS identifies several examples:

- Conti allocated $60,000 for a valid Cobalt Strike license;
- Testers received a budget of several thousand dollars per month for security and antivirus software; and
- Reverse Engineers were directed in July 2021 to focus on Windows 11, then Microsoft’s newest operating system. [SRC-003]

These details suggest an organized software-development and testing process. The available sources do not establish whether these expenditures were always made lawfully or whether every reported purchase was completed; they report them as findings from the leaked material.

### 3.5 Recruiting, finance, negotiation, and outside relationships

CIS places the Conti leaks in the context of a broader trend in cybercrime: criminal organizations adopting functions resembling legitimate corporations. The reported functions include recruiters, finance and accounting, and ransom negotiators. [SRC-003]

The RaaS structure also implies relationships beyond Conti’s central workforce:

- affiliates or intrusion operators;
- initial access brokers;
- outside spamming contractors;
- tool vendors or suppliers;
- victims and their representatives; and
- possibly other malware groups.

The evidence directly supports the existence of reported internal roles and a general RaaS relationship. It does not provide a complete list of affiliates, prove the identities of contractors, or establish the terms of particular commercial relationships.

## 4. Operational workflow reconstructed from the sources

The returned evidence supports the following generalized workflow:

### 4.1 Access and intrusion

Initial access could be obtained by Conti personnel, affiliates, or initial access brokers. CIS discusses IABs as participants in the wider RaaS ecosystem, but the returned excerpt does not identify specific Conti IABs or prove that every Conti intrusion used one. [SRC-003]

### 4.2 Deployment and encryption

After access, operators deployed Conti ransomware, encrypted servers and workstations, and disrupted the victim’s ability to use its systems. The DOJ describes Conti as malware that affected victim computers and networks by encrypting their data. [SRC-004]

### 4.3 Data theft and extortion

The Rewards for Justice account states that operators stole files before or alongside encryption. Victims were directed through a ransom letter to contact the operators through an online portal. If the ransom was not paid, stolen data could be published or sold through a site controlled by Conti actors. [SRC-001]

### 4.4 Negotiation and payment

The reported existence of negotiators and negotiation infrastructure indicates that victim communications were treated as a specialized operational function. CIS describes negotiators as coordinating ransom payments, while the Rewards for Justice account describes the portal-based process for completing transactions. [SRC-001] [SRC-003]

### 4.5 Public disclosure and pressure

The threat to publish or sell stolen data created a second pressure mechanism beyond system encryption. This is the double-extortion model identified by CIS. [SRC-003]

The sources do not reveal a complete standard operating procedure, a verified payment ledger, or a complete division of proceeds for individual cases.

## 5. Political statements, Russia, and the Ukraine-related disclosures

### 5.1 Public position after Russia’s invasion

Rapid7 reports that Conti initially pledged support for the Russian government after the invasion of Ukraine. Two days later, Conti issued a revised statement condemning the war and saying it would retaliate only if Russian critical infrastructure were targeted. [SRC-002]

Rewards for Justice likewise reports that Conti operators supported the Russian government and threatened critical infrastructure in countries perceived to be conducting cyberattacks or war against Russia. CIS states that Conti announced its “full support” for Russia after the February 24, 2022 invasion. [SRC-001] [SRC-003]

### 5.2 Internal disagreement

Rapid7 reports that some Conti members sided with Ukraine, causing internal strife. This indicates that the public pro-Russian position did not necessarily reflect a uniform view among all participants. [SRC-002]

The sources establish reported public statements and internal disagreement. They do not establish that the political statements were directed by the Russian government, that every member supported Russia, or that all Conti personnel operated under state control.

### 5.3 Meaning of “Russian government-linked”

The official U.S. description calls Conti Russian government-linked. That is an official attribution characterization. It should not be expanded beyond the wording supported by the source.

The returned sources do not provide:

- a specific Russian government agency;
- a named government officer;
- a verified command channel;
- a payment or tasking record; or
- a judicial finding that all Conti members acted under Russian government direction.

The record therefore supports reporting the official “Russian government-linked” characterization while preserving uncertainty about the precise nature of the relationship.

## 6. Infrastructure, recovery, shutdown, and possible successors

Rapid7 reports that Conti began taking down exposed infrastructure by March 2, 2022, after the chat disclosures. Rapid7 nevertheless assessed that Conti remained an active and significant threat because of its sophisticated capabilities, funding, and ability to recover from previously exposed infrastructure. On March 9, Rapid7 observed what it described as a resumption of normal operations. [SRC-002]

CIS later reports that Conti’s handlers began dismantling the operation. According to that account, the larger Conti platform shut down and rebranded into several smaller units, while approximately one month later its data-leak and negotiation infrastructure also shut down. [SRC-003]

These accounts are not necessarily irreconcilable:

- Rapid7 describes activity shortly after the leak.
- CIS describes later dismantling, fragmentation, and infrastructure shutdown.

However, the sources do not establish whether the later units were:

- formal successor organizations;
- rebranded portions of the same operation;
- groups composed of former Conti personnel; or
- independent organizations with no continuing legal or organizational identity.

The returned evidence therefore supports a chronology of apparent recovery followed by later fragmentation or shutdown reporting, but not a verified successor map.

## 7. Aliases and the public attribution record

### 7.1 Aliases identified by Rewards for Justice

Rewards for Justice identifies the following online aliases as malicious cyber actors believed to be linked to Conti and Wizard Spider:

- “Target”;
- “Reshaev”;
- “Professor”;
- “Tramp”; and
- “Dandis.”

The page associates them with Russia and offers a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification or location of qualifying actors involved in malicious cyber activity against U.S. critical infrastructure. [SRC-001]

The wording “believed to be linked” is significant. The source does not provide civilian names, photographs, confirmed dates of birth, or a judicial determination assigning each alias to a particular person.

### 7.2 Alleged developer referenced in the leaks

Rapid7 reports that @ContiLeaks named one alleged Conti developer and provided an email address and GitHub account. The returned source excerpt does not reproduce the person’s name or establish a civilian identity. No identity should be inferred from that reference. [SRC-002]

### 7.3 The unidentified leaker

Rapid7 assesses that the scale of the disclosure suggested the leaker was either:

- a very senior member of Conti; or
- a coalition of disgruntled Conti affiliates.

This is an intelligence assessment presenting alternatives, not a verified identification. The source does not resolve whether either explanation was correct. [SRC-002]

## 8. Law-enforcement records and identified defendants

### 8.1 Case 3:23-CR-00092

The DOJ Conti Ransomware page lists four defendants under case number `3:23-CR-00092`:

- Maksim Galochkin;
- Maksim Rudenskiy;
- Mikhail Tsarev; and
- Andrey Zhuykov.

The DOJ page states that they were charged on September 7, 2023, with:

- conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act; and
- conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The returned record does not show convictions or guilty pleas for these four defendants. The page expressly states that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. [SRC-004]

### 8.2 Case 3:23-CR-00088

The DOJ page lists Oleksii Lytvynenko under case number `3:23-CR-00088`. It states that he was charged on November 7, 2025, with conspiracy to deploy Conti, described as a ransomware variant that infected victim computers and networks and encrypted data. [SRC-004]

The same page states that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on June 10, 2026, to Count 2 of the indictment—conspiracy to commit wire fraud—under a plea agreement. The page states that sentencing was scheduled for September 10, 2026. The returned material does not provide the outcome of sentencing. [SRC-004]

### 8.3 What the DOJ records do and do not establish

The DOJ records establish that the United States brought Conti-related criminal charges against the named defendants and that Lytvynenko entered the specified guilty plea. They do not, in the returned material:

- map any defendant to “Target,” “Reshaev,” “Professor,” “Tramp,” or “Dandis”;
- identify the defendants’ internal Conti roles;
- establish that the four 2023 defendants were convicted;
- establish that the defendants were members of every organizational unit described in the leaks; or
- establish relationships among the defendants.

The appearance of a name in a Conti-related DOJ record is not, by itself, evidence that the person used one of the Rewards for Justice aliases or occupied a particular role in Conti.

## 9. Verified facts, allegations, assessments, and unresolved issues

### 9.1 Officially documented facts

The returned records officially document that:

- Rewards for Justice described Conti/Wizard Spider as a Russian government-linked RaaS group. [SRC-001]
- Rewards for Justice identified five aliases as actors believed to be linked to Conti. [SRC-001]
- The U.S. government offered a reward of up to $10 million for qualifying information. [SRC-001]
- DOJ charged Galochkin, Rudenskiy, Tsarev, and Zhuykov in 2023. [SRC-004]
- DOJ charged Lytvynenko in 2025. [SRC-004]
- Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on June 10, 2026, to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. [SRC-004]
- DOJ states that the other named defendants are presumed innocent. [SRC-004]

### 9.2 Investigative findings and intelligence assessments

The following are supported as reported investigative findings or assessments, but not as judicially established facts:

- Conti operated through specialized business units. [SRC-003]
- The organization employed Coders, Testers, Administrators, Reverse Engineers, and Penetration Testers/Hackers. [SRC-003]
- Negotiators handled ransom-payment coordination. [SRC-003]
- Spamming work was contracted outside the organization. [SRC-003]
- Conti maintained internal budgets and invested in testing and technical development. [SRC-003]
- Conti had apparent or reported ties to TrickBot. [SRC-001] [SRC-003]
- The leak came either from a senior member or from a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. [SRC-002]
- Conti resumed normal operations after initially taking down exposed infrastructure. [SRC-002]
- The larger operation later fragmented, rebranded, or shut down portions of its infrastructure. [SRC-003]

### 9.3 Unresolved questions

The returned evidence does not resolve:

- the civilian identities behind the five aliases;
- whether any alias corresponds to a named DOJ defendant;
- the identity of the alleged developer named by @ContiLeaks;
- the identity of the leaker;
- the precise structure of Conti’s leadership;
- the terms of specific affiliate agreements;
- the exact relationship between Conti and TrickBot;
- the precise relationship between Conti and the Russian government;
- whether later smaller units were genuine organizational successors;
- whether all leaked credentials and alleged infrastructure information were authentic; or
- why the official sources report different victim totals.

## 10. Conflicting accounts and how they should be interpreted

### 10.1 Activity after the February 2022 leak

Rapid7 observed a return to normal operations by March 9, 2022. CIS later reported that Conti’s larger platform shut down or fragmented. The most cautious interpretation is that the sources describe different phases: short-term recovery followed by later restructuring or dissolution. They do not prove either uninterrupted continuity or complete organizational disappearance. [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

### 10.2 Victim counts

Rewards for Justice reports more than 400 organizations worldwide, including more than 290 in the United States, in the described healthcare and first-responder context. DOJ reports more than 900 affected businesses, nonprofits, governments, and other victims worldwide. Because the sources do not explain their methodologies, neither figure should be used to invalidate the other. They should be presented as separate official descriptions with an unresolved difference in scope. [SRC-001] [SRC-004]

### 10.3 State linkage and internal political division

The U.S. government’s “Russian government-linked” characterization coexists with reporting that some Conti members supported Ukraine and that Conti revised its public statement. This does not necessarily contradict the attribution: a group can be described as linked to a state while containing internal dissent. But the returned evidence does not establish the form, strength, or universality of the state relationship. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

### 10.4 Alias attribution

The Rewards for Justice aliases and DOJ defendants appear in separate returned records. No returned source connects them. Treating them as identical would exceed the evidence.

## 11. Overall assessment as of October 1, 2026

The strongest evidence-based reconstruction is that Conti was a mature, commercially organized RaaS operation with centralized technical and business functions and distributed intrusion activity. It combined malware development, testing, operational hacking, administration, negotiation, stolen-data publication, and financial processes. The leaks reveal an organization that resembled a distributed criminal company more than an informal hacker collective.

The leaks also show the limits of public attribution. They provide operational detail without producing a complete verified identity structure. Public government records identify aliases as believed to be linked to Conti and separately identify defendants charged in Conti-related cases, but the returned sources do not connect those two sets of identities.

The legal record is clearest for procedural status. Four individuals were charged in 2023 and remain presumed innocent according to the DOJ page. Oleksii Lytvynenko pleaded guilty in 2026 to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The returned sources do not establish the final legal status of the other defendants or provide a full account of the factual admissions in Lytvynenko’s plea.

Thus, the public attribution record supports high confidence in Conti’s existence, RaaS business model, extortion workflow, and broad organizational specialization. It supports official attribution language concerning Russian government linkage and the five named aliases, but not a complete identity mapping or a fully documented command structure.
